parent.name: Answer matcher
parent.one_liner: Finds the landlord's saved answer, or admits there is none.
parent.explain: I decide whether a landlord already answered a renter's question, using plain code with no AI model. That means the same question always gets the same result. I turn each question into key words, then weigh each word by how rare it is across all saved questions. I score a pair of questions as the average of overlap and coverage, and I require a shared topic word. At 0.5 or higher I return the saved answer word for word; below that I answer nothing and offer to ask the landlord.
parent.why: A confident wrong answer about a deposit or a pet rule can mislead a renter, so I only answer when the match is strong. Plain code gives the same result every time, which lets me pin each tricky case in a test. A miss just means a short wait for the landlord.

children.name: Key words and synonyms
children.one_liner: Turns a question into a small set of canonical key words.
children.explain: I lower-case a question and pull out its words. I drop filler words like 'the' and 'is' (the STOPWORDS list), and listing ids like A201. I fold variants into one canonical word using SYNONYMS, so dog, cats and animal all become pet. Car, garage and driveway all become parking. Words with no synonym get a light stem, which cuts a plural 's' or turns 'ies' into 'y'.
children.why: Renters never phrase a question as a landlord saved it, so raw matching would miss 'can I park my car?' against 'Is parking available?'. Folding variants lets different wording land on the same word. Dropping filler keeps empty words from looking like a topic.

children.name: Rarity weights (IDF)
children.one_liner: Rare words count more than words every question uses.
children.explain: I count, for every word, how many saved questions use it; that count is its document frequency (df). The weight is log((n+1)/(df+1)) + 1, where n is the number of saved questions. A word used by fewer questions weighs more: with the 23 demo questions, parking is 2.39 and rent 2.10. A word no saved question uses counts as rare, so it gets the biggest weight I have computed. I count over every landlord's saved questions, not just the one being asked.
children.why: Without weights every shared word would count the same, and 'rent' or 'included' would drive a match as much as 'parking'. Weighting by rarity makes the distinctive topic word matter most. Unseen words count as rare so a renter's new word is never treated like filler.

children.name: Overlap and coverage
children.one_liner: Scores a pair of questions by overlap and coverage.
children.explain: I score a renter's question against one saved question using the weights of their key words. Overlap is the shared weight divided by the weight of all words in either question. Coverage is the shared weight divided by the weight of the renter's words only. The score is the average of the two, 0.5 * (overlap + coverage). So a short question like 'can I park?' that a longer saved one fully covers still scores 0.68.
children.why: Overlap alone punishes short questions: 'can I park?' shares one word with a long saved question, so overlap is small. Coverage fixes that by asking how much of the renter's own question the saved one explains. Averaging keeps a long saved question from matching on one lucky word.

children.name: Topic-word guard
children.one_liner: Requires a shared topic word, not just words like 'rent'.
children.explain: I keep a short list of GENERIC words: include, rent, cost, allow, month, schedule and sign. A match needs at least one shared word that is not on that list, or I score it 0. This fixed a bug where 'is parking included in rent?' got the utilities answer, matching only on 'include' and 'rent'. It also stops 'is that allowed?' from matching 'are pets allowed?'. Two tests pin both cases: A201 and 'Is that allowed?'.
children.why: A high score on common words is a false friend, because 'include' and 'rent' appear in many saved questions. Giving a renter the utilities answer to a parking question is a confident wrong answer, the worst failure here. Requiring a topic word makes the match mean something.

children.name: Fail-safe threshold
children.one_liner: Below 0.5 I stay silent and offer to ask the landlord.
children.explain: I answer only when the best score is at least MATCH_THRESHOLD, which is 0.5, and then I return the saved answer word for word. Below that I mark it not_answered, do not guess, and send it to the landlord only if the renter says yes. A score of 0.25 or more, the RELATED_FLOOR, also shows a related saved answer with a caution that it is not the same question. When two saved answers tie, the listing-specific one wins.
children.why: A wrong answer about a deposit or a pet rule can mislead a renter, while a miss only costs a short wait for the landlord. So a miss fails safe and nothing is said as fact. The related answer carries a warning, so a near miss still helps without pretending to be the answer.
